Build it as a rules engine first, document engine second, AI layer third.

I’d like this to a desktop app or even some sort of plug in. Propose paths. But I want it marketable

That order matters. If you start with “AI that formats legal documents,” you’ll get inconsistent junk. If you start with deterministic rules, you get something lawyers can trust.

The core idea

Your legal formatting and structure engine should take in:
• document type
• jurisdiction
• court level
• raw text or drafted sections
• party/case metadata

And return:
• a correctly structured document
• normalized headings
• a proper caption
• section order validation
• formatting corrections
• warnings where something is missing or inconsistent

So the product is not “write a brief.”
It is:

“Take messy legal content and force it into a valid, polished, court-usable structure.”

That is a real product.

⸻

System architecture
Use a modular design with five layers:

Layer 1: Input layer

This accepts:
• pasted draft text
• uploaded motion/brief text
• metadata fields
• optional style preferences

Example metadata:
• jurisdiction: Wisconsin
• court: Court of Appeals
• document_type: appellant_brief
• case_name: State v. Christopherson
• case_number: 2024AP1234-CR
• party_role: defendant-appellant

This layer should be dumb and clean. Just ingest and normalize.

⸻

Layer 2: Rules layer

This is the heart of the engine.

It stores deterministic rules for:
• captions
• heading formats
• required sections
• section order
• numbering schemes
• signature block format
• certifications
• margins, fonts, spacing if you are generating a finished file

This should be jurisdiction-specific.

Example:
• wi_appellate_brief_rules
• wi_circuit_motion_rules
• federal_district_motion_rules

Do not hard-code everything into the same file. Use separate templates/rulesets.

⸻

Layer 3: Structure parser

This analyzes the incoming draft and identifies:
• existing headings
• section boundaries
• caption-like text
• signature block
• citations
• numbering patterns

This parser converts a messy document into a structured internal representation.

Example internal model:

{
"caption": {...},
"sections": [
{"type": "statement_of_case", "heading": "STATEMENT OF THE CASE", "content": "..."},
{"type": "facts", "heading": "STATEMENT OF FACTS", "content": "..."},
{"type": "argument", "heading": "ARGUMENT", "content": "..."}
],
"signature_block": {...},
"certifications": [...]
}

This is what lets the engine manipulate documents reliably.

⸻

Layer 4: Formatter/validator

This layer compares the parsed document against the applicable rules and then:
• inserts missing sections
• renames headings
• reorders sections
• standardizes numbering
• generates or repairs captions
• flags formatting violations
• optionally rewrites boilerplate labels only

Important: this layer should mostly be deterministic.

For example:
• “Argument” becomes “ARGUMENT”
• “statement of facts” becomes “STATEMENT OF FACTS”
• Heading level 2 becomes “I.” or “A.” depending on rules
• Missing “Conclusion” gets flagged or inserted as a placeholder

⸻

Layer 5: Output layer

This produces:
• clean markdown
• HTML
• DOCX
• maybe PDF later

DOCX matters most for legal users.

You should preserve:
• section hierarchy
• indentation
• font rules
• line spacing
• page breaks where needed

⸻

What the engine actually does
Here are the first real features I’d build.

A. Caption engine

This takes party/court metadata and outputs a formatted caption.

Inputs:
• court name
• case title
• docket number
• party names and roles
• document title

Outputs:
• jurisdiction-specific caption block

This is one of the easiest and most useful components to build first.

⸻

B. Heading engine

This does:
• detect heading levels
• normalize heading capitalization
• enforce numbering patterns
• align headings to chosen template

Examples:
• top-level heading: all caps
• second-level heading: Roman numeral
• third-level heading: capital letter
• fourth-level heading: numbered subsection

You need a heading schema.

Example:

{
"level_1": {"style": "ALL_CAPS_CENTERED"},
"level_2": {"style": "ROMAN_NUMERAL_TITLE_CASE"},
"level_3": {"style": "CAPITAL_LETTER_SENTENCE_CASE"},
"level_4": {"style": "ARABIC_NUMERAL_SENTENCE_CASE"}
}

⸻

C. Section-order engine

This checks whether required sections exist and whether they are in the right order.

For a Wisconsin appellate brief, for example, your engine should know the expected sequence and flag:
• missing Statement of Issues
• Facts before Case
• missing certifications
• malformed conclusion

This is pure rules logic. No AI needed.

⸻

D. Citation consistency engine

Do not try to solve all Bluebook at once.

Start narrower:
• consistent case-name formatting
• consistent short cites
• consistent use of Id. or not
• consistent spacing and punctuation

This engine should detect patterns and inconsistencies, then either:
• auto-correct simple problems
• flag complex ones

That is already valuable.

⸻

E. Boilerplate block engine

This generates routine standardized blocks:
• signature block
• certificate of service
• word-count certification
• appendix certification
• motion intro block
• notice sections

This is low-risk and high-utility.

⸻

Internal data model
Do not manipulate raw text blindly. Convert documents into a structured representation first.

A good internal model might include:

{
"document_type": "appellate_brief",
"jurisdiction": "wisconsin",
"court_level": "court_of_appeals",
"metadata": {
"case_name": "State v. Smith",
"case_number": "2025AP1234-CR",
"document_title": "Brief of Defendant-Appellant"
},
"caption": {...},
"sections": [...],
"certifications": [...],
"signature_block": {...},
"format_profile": {
"font": "Times New Roman",
"line_spacing": "double",
"margins": "1in"
}
}

Once you have that, everything gets easier.

⸻

Repo structure
I’d build the repo like this:

legal-format-engine/
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
├── .env.example
├── src/
│ └── legal_format_engine/
│ ├── api/
│ │ ├── server.py
│ │ └── routes.py
│ ├── models/
│ │ ├── document.py
│ │ ├── caption.py
│ │ └── section.py
│ ├── parsers/
│ │ ├── plain_text_parser.py
│ │ ├── markdown_parser.py
│ │ └── docx_parser.py
│ ├── rules/
│ │ ├── base.py
│ │ ├── wisconsin/
│ │ │ ├── appellate_brief.py
│ │ │ ├── circuit_motion.py
│ │ │ └── caption_rules.py
│ │ └── federal/
│ ├── engines/
│ │ ├── caption_engine.py
│ │ ├── heading_engine.py
│ │ ├── section_engine.py
│ │ ├── citation_engine.py
│ │ └── validator.py
│ ├── renderers/
│ │ ├── markdown_renderer.py
│ │ ├── html_renderer.py
│ │ └── docx_renderer.py
│ └── utils/
│ ├── text.py
│ └── numbering.py
├── tests/
│ ├── rules/
│ ├── engines/
│ └── fixtures/
└── docs/
├── architecture.md
├── rulesets.md
└── roadmap.md

Python is a good fit here.

⸻

How the rules should be written
Use declarative rules, not spaghetti code.

For example, a ruleset file could look like:

RULESET = {
"document_type": "wisconsin_appellate_brief",
"required_sections": [
"statement_of_issues",
"statement_of_case",
"statement_of_facts",
"argument",
"conclusion",
"certification"
],
"section_order": [
"statement_of_issues",
"statement_of_case",
"statement_of_facts",
"argument",
"conclusion",
"certification"
],
"heading_style": {
"level_1": "all_caps_centered",
"level_2": "roman_numeral",
"level_3": "capital_letter"
},
"font": "Times New Roman",
"line_spacing": "double"
}

That lets you add new jurisdictions later without rewriting the engine.

⸻

Where AI belongs
Use AI only where deterministic rules break down.

Good AI uses:
• classify whether a heading is actually “facts” or “case”
• suggest better heading phrasing
• detect likely missing sections from content
• compare style consistency across the draft

Bad AI uses:
• deciding court formatting rules from scratch
• inventing captions
• reordering legal sections without explicit rules
• rewriting citations freely

The core engine should work even if the AI layer is off.

That is the standard you want.

⸻

MVP build order
Here’s the right sequence.

Phase 1: deterministic MVP

Build these first:
• caption generator
• heading normalizer
• section validator
• section reorderer
• boilerplate block generator

That alone is useful and sellable.

Phase 2: document ingestion/output

Add:
• DOCX parsing
• DOCX rendering
• style-preserving export

Phase 3: citation and style checks

Add:
• citation consistency checker
• defined-term consistency
• capitalization consistency

Phase 4: AI assist layer

Add:
• heading suggestions
• section classification
• advanced cleanup recommendations

Phase 5: premium writing tier

Then build:
• argument structure suggestions
• legal synthesis modules
• advanced draft support

⸻

API / connector functions
If this is exposed as an MCP-style toolset, your first tools should be concrete.

Examples:
• generate_caption
• normalize_headings
• validate_document_structure
• reorder_sections
• generate_signature_block
• generate_certification
• check_citation_consistency
• apply_format_profile

Those are real tools. Lawyers can understand them instantly.

Avoid vague tools like:
• improve_brief
• make_document_better

That language kills trust.

⸻

How to sell it
Your entry-level offer is not “AI legal writer.”

It is:

“A legal document formatting and structure engine that turns rough drafts into court-ready briefs and motions.”

That is clearer, safer, and easier to trust.

Then your premium tier becomes:

“Advanced legal writing support built on top of the formatting engine.”

That ladder makes sense.

⸻

Biggest mistakes to avoid
Do not:
• start with all jurisdictions
• promise full Bluebook perfection
• lead with AI writing
• rely on one giant prompt
• manipulate raw text without parsing structure
• mix research, writing, and formatting into one service

You want separate modules that can talk to each other.

⸻

The best first niche
You should start with one narrow lane:
• Wisconsin appellate briefs
or
• Wisconsin criminal motions

Not both at once.

Given your background, Wisconsin appellate work is the sharper wedge. You know exactly what “good” looks like there.

⸻

What I would build first, concretely
If I were building your v1 this week, I’d do this:
1. generate_caption
2. normalize_headings
3. validate_wi_appellate_sections
4. generate_certification_block
5. export_docx

That’s enough for a demo and enough to prove demand.

After that:
6. check_citation_consistency
7. section_classifier
8. signature_block_generator

That is a serious starting product.

If you want, I’ll turn this into a concrete product blueprint with:
• exact modules
• exact functions
• sample input/output
• and a development roadmap for a Wisconsin appellate MVP.

Show more

7. No persistence. Every time you close and reopen the panel, all fields are blank (except defaults). Attorney info should persist via Office.context.roamingSettings.

Architecture: 4-Layer ML Pipeline
Upload (any format) → Normalizer → Feature Extractor → Learner → Synthesizer

Layer 1: Normalizer (ml/normalizer.py)
The equalizer you asked for. Every document — DOCX, PDF, .doc, HTML — gets stripped down to the same canonical representation. Quirks that would infect learning:

Problem	Solution
PDF says "TimesNewRomanPSMT"	Mapped to "Times New Roman" (50+ font variants handled)
PDF margin estimated at 0.97"	Snapped to 1.0" (standard legal margin)
DOCX has font size 11.8pt	Snapped to 12pt (standard legal size)
PDF line spacing computed as 2.07	Snapped to 2.0 (double)
Each format has different confidence	DOCX=1.0, PDF=0.6, HTML=0.7, .doc=0.4
Layer 2: Feature Extractor (ml/features.py)
Converts normalized documents into weighted feature vectors. PDF margins automatically get lower weight (0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36) than DOCX margins (1.0).

Layer 3: Learner (ml/learner.py)
Weighted statistical learning with outlier rejection:

Numerical features: weighted median + IQR outlier rejection
Categorical features: weighted voting
One badly formatted brief won't infect the model
DOCX features outweigh PDF features (higher confidence)
Layer 4: Synthesizer (ml/synthesizer.py)
Generates YAML rulesets from learned patterns
Diffs against existing rulesets with confidence-scored recommendations
Never silently overrides court rules — produces suggestions

That order matters. If you start with “AI that formats legal documents,” you’ll get inconsistent junk. If you start with deterministic rules, you get something lawyers can trust.

The core idea

Your legal formatting and structure engine should take in:
• document type
• jurisdiction
• court level
• raw text or drafted sections
• party/case metadata

And return:
• a correctly structured document
• normalized headings
• a proper caption
• section order validation
• formatting corrections
• warnings where something is missing or inconsistent

So the product is not “write a brief.”
It is:

“Take messy legal content and force it into a valid, polished, court-usable structure.”

That is a real product.

⸻

System architecture
Use a modular design with five layers:

Layer 1: Input layer

This accepts:
• pasted draft text
• uploaded motion/brief text
• metadata fields
• optional style preferences

Example metadata:
• jurisdiction: Wisconsin
• court: Court of Appeals
• document_type: appellant_brief
• case_name: State v. Christopherson
• case_number: 2024AP1234-CR
• party_role: defendant-appellant

This layer should be dumb and clean. Just ingest and normalize.

⸻

Layer 2: Rules layer

This is the heart of the engine.

It stores deterministic rules for:
• captions
• heading formats
• required sections
• section order
• numbering schemes
• signature block format
• certifications
• margins, fonts, spacing if you are generating a finished file

This should be jurisdiction-specific.

Example:
• wi_appellate_brief_rules
• wi_circuit_motion_rules
• federal_district_motion_rules

Do not hard-code everything into the same file. Use separate templates/rulesets.

⸻

Layer 3: Structure parser

This analyzes the incoming draft and identifies:
• existing headings
• section boundaries
• caption-like text
• signature block
• citations
• numbering patterns

This parser converts a messy document into a structured internal representation.

Example internal model:

{
"caption": {...},
"sections": [
{"type": "statement_of_case", "heading": "STATEMENT OF THE CASE", "content": "..."},
{"type": "facts", "heading": "STATEMENT OF FACTS", "content": "..."},
{"type": "argument", "heading": "ARGUMENT", "content": "..."}
],
"signature_block": {...},
"certifications": [...]
}

This is what lets the engine manipulate documents reliably.

⸻

Layer 4: Formatter/validator

This layer compares the parsed document against the applicable rules and then:
• inserts missing sections
• renames headings
• reorders sections
• standardizes numbering
• generates or repairs captions
• flags formatting violations
• optionally rewrites boilerplate labels only

Important: this layer should mostly be deterministic.

For example:
• “Argument” becomes “ARGUMENT”
• “statement of facts” becomes “STATEMENT OF FACTS”
• Heading level 2 becomes “I.” or “A.” depending on rules
• Missing “Conclusion” gets flagged or inserted as a placeholder

⸻

Layer 5: Output layer

This produces:
• clean markdown
• HTML
• DOCX
• maybe PDF later

DOCX matters most for legal users.

You should preserve:
• section hierarchy
• indentation
• font rules
• line spacing
• page breaks where needed

⸻

What the engine actually does
Here are the first real features I’d build.

A. Caption engine

This takes party/court metadata and outputs a formatted caption.

Inputs:
• court name
• case title
• docket number
• party names and roles
• document title

Outputs:
• jurisdiction-specific caption block

This is one of the easiest and most useful components to build first.

⸻

B. Heading engine

This does:
• detect heading levels
• normalize heading capitalization
• enforce numbering patterns
• align headings to chosen template

Examples:
• top-level heading: all caps
• second-level heading: Roman numeral
• third-level heading: capital letter
• fourth-level heading: numbered subsection

You need a heading schema.

Example:

{
"level_1": {"style": "ALL_CAPS_CENTERED"},
"level_2": {"style": "ROMAN_NUMERAL_TITLE_CASE"},
"level_3": {"style": "CAPITAL_LETTER_SENTENCE_CASE"},
"level_4": {"style": "ARABIC_NUMERAL_SENTENCE_CASE"}
}

⸻

C. Section-order engine

This checks whether required sections exist and whether they are in the right order.

For a Wisconsin appellate brief, for example, your engine should know the expected sequence and flag:
• missing Statement of Issues
• Facts before Case
• missing certifications
• malformed conclusion

This is pure rules logic. No AI needed.

⸻

D. Citation consistency engine

Do not try to solve all Bluebook at once.

Start narrower:
• consistent case-name formatting
• consistent short cites
• consistent use of Id. or not
• consistent spacing and punctuation

This engine should detect patterns and inconsistencies, then either:
• auto-correct simple problems
• flag complex ones

That is already valuable.

⸻

E. Boilerplate block engine

This generates routine standardized blocks:
• signature block
• certificate of service
• word-count certification
• appendix certification
• motion intro block
• notice sections

This is low-risk and high-utility.

⸻

Internal data model
Do not manipulate raw text blindly. Convert documents into a structured representation first.

A good internal model might include:

{
"document_type": "appellate_brief",
"jurisdiction": "wisconsin",
"court_level": "court_of_appeals",
"metadata": {
"case_name": "State v. Smith",
"case_number": "2025AP1234-CR",
"document_title": "Brief of Defendant-Appellant"
},
"caption": {...},
"sections": [...],
"certifications": [...],
"signature_block": {...},
"format_profile": {
"font": "Times New Roman",
"line_spacing": "double",
"margins": "1in"
}
}

⸻

How the rules should be written
Use declarative rules, not spaghetti code.

For example, a ruleset file could look like:

RULESET = {
"document_type": "wisconsin_appellate_brief",
"required_sections": [
"statement_of_issues",
"statement_of_case",
"statement_of_facts",
"argument",
"conclusion",
"certification"
],
"section_order": [
"statement_of_issues",
"statement_of_case",
"statement_of_facts",
"argument",
"conclusion",
"certification"
],
"heading_style": {
"level_1": "all_caps_centered",
"level_2": "roman_numeral",
"level_3": "capital_letter"
},
"font": "Times New Roman",
"line_spacing": "double"
}

That lets you add new jurisdictions later without rewriting the engine.

⸻

Where AI belongs
Use AI only where deterministic rules break down.

Good AI uses:
• classify whether a heading is actually “facts” or “case”
• suggest better heading phrasing
• detect likely missing sections from content
• compare style consistency across the draft

Bad AI uses:
• deciding court formatting rules from scratch
• inventing captions
• reordering legal sections without explicit rules
• rewriting citations freely

The core engine should work even if the AI layer is off.

That is the standard you want.

⸻

MVP build order
Here’s the right sequence.

Phase 1: deterministic MVP

Build these first:
• caption generator
• heading normalizer
• section validator
• section reorderer
• boilerplate block generator

That alone is useful and sellable.

Phase 2: document ingestion/output

Add:
• DOCX parsing
• DOCX rendering
• style-preserving export

Phase 3: citation and style checks

Add:
• citation consistency checker
• defined-term consistency
• capitalization consistency

Phase 4: AI assist layer

Add:
• heading suggestions
• section classification
• advanced cleanup recommendations

Phase 5: premium writing tier

Then build:
• argument structure suggestions
• legal synthesis modules
• advanced draft support

⸻

API / connector functions
If this is exposed as an MCP-style toolset, your first tools should be concrete.

Examples:
• generate_caption
• normalize_headings
• validate_document_structure
• reorder_sections
• generate_signature_block
• generate_certification
• check_citation_consistency
• apply_format_profile

Those are real tools. Lawyers can understand them instantly.

Avoid vague tools like:
• improve_brief
• make_document_better

That language kills trust.

⸻

How to sell it
Your entry-level offer is not “AI legal writer.”

It is:

“A legal document formatting and structure engine that turns rough drafts into court-ready briefs and motions.”

That is clearer, safer, and easier to trust.

Then your premium tier becomes:

“Advanced legal writing support built on top of the formatting engine.”

That ladder makes sense.

⸻

Biggest mistakes to avoid
Do not:
• start with all jurisdictions
• promise full Bluebook perfection
• lead with AI writing
• rely on one giant prompt
• manipulate raw text without parsing structure
• mix research, writing, and formatting into one service

You want separate modules that can talk to each other.

⸻

The best first niche
You should start with one narrow lane:
• Wisconsin appellate briefs
or
• Wisconsin criminal motions

Not both at once.

Given your background, Wisconsin appellate work is the sharper wedge. You know exactly what “good” looks like there.

Good question. Here are your options from simplest to most production-ready:

Option 1: Local Server (Current Setup)

Works offline
Cons:

Only works on the machine running the server
Can't share with other SPD attorneys

Option 2: Cloud VPS (DigitalOcean, Linode, Vultr, etc.)
How it works: You rent a small Linux server for $5-12/month, run the API there. The Add-in manifest points to https://your-domain.com/api instead of localhost.

Pros:

Always running — no starting/stopping
Access from any machine with Word
Can share with other attorneys (just give them the manifest)
Your own server, full control
Cons:

$5-12/month
You manage the server (updates, security)
Documents travel over the internet (but HTTPS encrypted)

Run uvicorn behind it with systemd so it auto-starts
Update the manifest URLs to https://api.anchorfilings.com
Option 3: Platform-as-a-Service (Railway, Render, Fly.io)
How it works: You push your code, they handle servers, HTTPS, restarts, everything.

Pros:

No server management at all — just git push
Auto-HTTPS, auto-restarts, auto-scaling
Free tiers available (Railway: $5 credit/mo, Render: free tier with sleep, Fly.io: small free allowance)
Easiest path to "always on"
Cons:

Free tiers sleep after inactivity (5-15 min cold start on first request)
Paid tiers are $5-7/month for always-on
Slightly less control than your own VPS
Documents pass through their infrastructure

Here are your step-by-step instructions to install the Word Add-in. I'm providing both Windows and Mac paths — use whichever matches your setup.

Step 1: Clone the repo on your desktop
git clone https://github.com/nicksmithg/legal-format-engine.git
cd legal-format-engine
git checkout claude/legal-rules-engine-T9ZP3

Step 2: Install Python dependencies
pip install -e .

This installs the engine, FastAPI, uvicorn, and all dependencies.

Step 3: Generate HTTPS certificates with mkcert
Office.js requires HTTPS. mkcert creates locally-trusted certs.

Install mkcert:

Windows (with Chocolatey): choco install mkcert
Windows (with Scoop): scoop install mkcert
Mac: brew install mkcert
Then generate certs:

mkcert -install
mkcert -cert-file cert.pem -key-file key.pem localhost 127.0.0.1

This creates cert.pem and key.pem in your current directory. Keep them in the repo root.

Step 4: Start the server
uvicorn legal_format_engine.api.server:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8443 --ssl-certfile cert.pem --ssl-keyfile key.pem

Verify it's working: open https://localhost:8443/api/health in your browser. You should see {"status":"ok","version":"0.1.0"}.

Also verify the add-in page loads: https://localhost:8443/addin/taskpane.html

Leave this terminal running.

Step 5: Sideload the manifest into Word
Copy word-addin/manifest.xml to Word's sideload folder:

Windows:

# Create the folder if it doesn't exist
mkdir "$env:USERPROFILE\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Word\Wef" -Force

# Copy the manifest
copy word-addin\manifest.xml "$env:USERPROFILE\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Word\Wef\manifest.xml"

Mac:

# Create the folder if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p ~/Library/Containers/com.microsoft.Word/Data/Documents/wef

# Copy the manifest
cp word-addin/manifest.xml ~/Library/Containers/com.microsoft.Word/Data/Documents/wef/manifest.xml

Step 6: Load the Add-in in Word
Close Word completely if it's open, then reopen it
Open a new blank document (or an existing brief)
Go to Insert tab → My Add-ins (or Get Add-ins → My Add-ins tab)
You should see Legal Format Engine listed under "Developer Add-ins" or "Shared Folder"
Click it → Add
The taskpane will appear on the right side of Word with the collapsible sections: Case Info, Parties, Attorney, Letterhead, and Options.

Step 7: Use it
Paste or type your brief content into the Word document
Fill in the case info, parties, and attorney fields in the taskpane
Optionally create/select a letterhead
Click Format Brief
Confirm in the dialog
The engine formats your document and replaces it with the court-ready DOCX
Quick troubleshooting
Problem	Fix
Browser says "not secure" for localhost	Run mkcert -install again, restart browser
Add-in doesn't appear in My Add-ins	Make sure Word was fully closed and reopened after copying the manifest
"Cannot connect to server" in taskpane	Make sure uvicorn is running on port 8443 with SSL
Taskpane shows blank	Check https://localhost:8443/addin/taskpane.html loads in browser first

Here's the roadmap from where you are now to the Microsoft Store (AppSource):

1. Get a Microsoft Partner Center account
Sign up at Partner Center (partner.microsoft.com)
One-time registration fee (~$19)
You'll need a business identity — your startup works for this
2. Move from localhost to a real server
Deploy to Railway, Render, or Azure (we discussed this before)
Get a real domain (e.g., app.yourstartup.com)
Set up real SSL (Let's Encrypt, free)
Update manifest.xml to point to your production URL instead of https://localhost:8443
3. Prepare the manifest for submission
The simplified manifest works for sideloading, but the store version needs the full VersionOverrides back — with real icons (16x16, 32x32, 80x80 PNG files)
Add a proper support URL, privacy policy URL, and terms of use
You'll need marketing assets: app logo, screenshots, description
4. Validate the manifest
Microsoft provides a validation tool: run npx office-addin-manifest validate word-addin/manifest.xml (requires Node.js)
Or use their online validator
5. Submit to Partner Center
Upload the manifest
Fill in the listing: description, categories, screenshots, pricing (free or paid)
Select target markets (US, etc.)
Submit for review
6. Microsoft review process
Takes 1-2 weeks typically
They test functionality, security, and compliance
Common rejection reasons: broken features, missing privacy policy, UI issues
You may need to go back and forth a couple times

Architecture: 4-Layer ML Pipeline
Upload (any format) → Normalizer → Feature Extractor → Learner → Synthesizer

Layer 1: Normalizer (ml/normalizer.py)

Problem	Solution
PDF says "TimesNewRomanPSMT"	Mapped to "Times New Roman" (50+ font variants handled)

DOCX has font size 11.8pt	Snapped to 12pt (standard legal size)

Layer 2: Feature Extractor (ml/features.py)
Converts normalized documents into weighted feature vectors. PDF margins automatically get lower weight (0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36) than DOCX margins (1.0).

Weighted statistical learning with outlier rejection:

Numerical features: weighted median + IQR outlier rejection
Categorical features: weighted voting
One badly formatted brief won't infect the model
